knurly: Full of knots; hard; tough; hence, capable of enduring or resisting much.
knobby: 1. Full of, or covered with, knobs or hard protuberances. Dr. H. More. 2. Irregular; stubborn in particulars. (old) The informers continued in a knobby kind of obstinacy. Howell. 3. Abounding in rounded hills or mountains; hilly. [U.S.] Bartlett.
knit: 1. To form into a knot, or into knots; to tie together, as cord; to fasten by tying. A great sheet knit at the four corners. Acts x. 11. When your head did but ache, I knit my handkercher about your… | 1. To form a fabric by interlacing yarn or thread; to weave by making knots or loops. 2. To be united closely; to grow together; as, broken bones will in time knit and become sound.
knifeedge: A piece of steel sharpened to an acute edge or angle, and resting on a smooth surface, serving as the axis of motion of a pendulum, scale beam, or other piece required to oscillate with the least possible friction. Knife-edge file. See Illust. of File.
knowingly: 1. With knowledge; in a knowing manner; intelligently; consciously; deliberately; as, he would not knowingly offend. Strype. 2. By experience. (old) Shak.
knockoutdrops: Drops of some drug put in one's drink to stupefy him for purpose of robbery, etc. [Slang, U. S.]
knowing: 1. Skilful; well informed; intelligent; as, a knowing man; a knowing dog. The knowing and intelligent part of the world. South. 2. Artful; cunning; as, a knowing rascal. [Colloq.] | Knowledge; hence, experience. " In my knowing." Shak. This sore night Hath trifled former knowings. Shak.
knoppern: A kind of gall produced by a gallfly on the cup of an acorn, -- used in tanning and dyeing.
knifeboard: A board on which knives are cleaned or polished.
knitter: One who, or that which, knits, joins, or unites; a knitting machine. Shak.
knitch: A number of things tied or knit together; a bundle; a fagot. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Halliwell. When they [stems of asphodel] be dried, they ought to be made up into knitchets, or handfuls. Holland.
knap: A protuberance; a swelling; a knob; a button; hence, rising ground; a summit. See Knob, and Knop. The highest part and knap of the same island. Holland. | 1. To bite; to bite off; to break short. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. ] He will knap the spears apieces with his teeth. Dr. H. More. He breaketh the bow, and knappeth the spear in sunder. Ps. xlvi.
knitting: 1. The work of a knitter; the network formed by knitting. 2. Union formed by knitting, as of bones. Knitting machine, one of a number of contrivances for mechanically knitting stockings, jerseys, and the like. -- Knitting , a stiff rod, as of steel wire, with rounded ends for knitting yarn or threads into a fabric, as in stockings.
knacker: 1. One who makes knickknacks, toys, etc. Mortimer. 2. One of two or more pieces of bone or wood held loosely between the fingers, and struck together by moving the hand; -- called also clapper. | 1. a harness maker. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Halliwell. 2. One who slaughters worn-out horses and sells their flesh for dog's meat. [Eng.]
kneadable: That may be kneaded; capable of being worked into a mass.
knighthead: A bollard timber. See under Bollard.
kneehigh: Rising or reaching upward to the knees; as, the water is knee- high.
knowleche: See Knowl, edge. We consider and knowleche that we have offended. Chaucer.
know: 1. To perceive or apprehend clearly and certainly; to understand; to have full information of; as, to know one's duty. O, that a man might know The end of this day's business ere it come! Shak. | 1. To have knowledge; to have a clear and certain perception; to possess wisdom, instruction, or information; -- often with of. Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider. Is. i. 3.
knightservice: A tenure of lands held by knights on condition of performing military service. See Chivalry, n., 4. KNIGHT SERVICE; KNIGHT'S SERVICE Knight service. Also Knight's service. 1. (Feud. Law) The military service by rendering which a knight held his lands; also, the tenure of lands held on condition of performing military service.
knifeswitch: A switch consisting of one or more knifelike pieces hinged at one end and making contact near the other with flat gripping springs.
knacky: Having a knack; cunning; crafty; trickish. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Halliwell.
knockings: Large lumps picked out of the sieve, in dressing ore.
knotted: 1. Full of knots; having knots knurled; as, a knotted cord; the knotted oak. Dryden. 2. Interwoven; matted; entangled. Make . . . thy knotted and combined locks to part. Shak. 3. Having intersecting lines or figures. The west corner of thy curious knotted garden. Shak. 4.
knavish: 1. Like or characteristic of a knave; given to knavery; trickish; fraudulent; dishonest; villainous; as, a knavish fellow, or a knavish trick. "Knavish politicians." Macaulay. 2. Mischievous; roguish; waggish. Cupid is knavish lad, Thus to make poor females mad. Shak.
knockstone: A block upon which ore is broken up.
kneepan: A roundish, flattened, sesamoid bone in the tendon in front of the knee joint; the patella; the kneecap.
knobbler: The hart in its second year; a young deer. [Written also knobber.] Halliwell. He has hallooed the hounds upon a velvet-headed knobbler. Sir W. Scott.
knicker: A small ball of clay, baked hard and oiled, used as a marble by boys in playing. [Prov. Eng. & U. S.] Halliwell. Bartlett.
knockoff: That knocks off; of or pertaining to knocking off. | Act or place of knocking off; that which knocks off; specif. (Mach.), a cam or the like for disconnecting something, as a device in a knitting machine to remove loops from the needles.
knockknee: A condition in which the knees are bent in so as to touch each other in walking; inknee.
knaveship: A small due, in meal, established by usage, which is paid to the under miller. [Scot.]
knobbed: Containing knobs; full of knobs; ending in a nob. See Illust of Antenna. The horns of a roe deer of Greenland are pointed at the top, and knobbed or tuberous at the bottom. Grew.
knavery: 1. The practices of a knave; petty villainy; fraud; trickery; a knavish action. This is flat knavery, to take upon you another man's name. Shak. 2. pl. Roguish or mischievous tricks. Shak.
knab: 1. To seize with the teeth; to gnaw. "Knabbing crusts." (old) L'Estrange. 2. To nab. See Nab, v. t. [Colloq.]
knell: The stoke of a bell tolled at a funeral or at the death of a person; a death signal; a passing bell; hence, figuratively, a warning of, or a sound indicating, the passing away of anything. | To sound as a knell; especially, to toll at a death or funeral; hence, to sound as a warning or evil omen. Not worth a blessing nor a bell to knell for thee. Beau. & Fl.
knoller: One who tolls a bell. (old) Sherwood.
knackish: Trickish; artful. (old) -- Knack"ish*ness, n. (old) Dr. H. More.
knavishly: 1. In a knavish manner; dishonestly; fraudulently. Holland. 2. Mischievously; waggishly; roguishly. "Knavishly witty." Gayton.
kneed: 1. Having knees;- used chiefly in composition; as, in-kneed; out- kneed; weak-kneed. 2. (Bot.) Geniculated; forming an obtuse angle at the joints, like the knee when a little bent; as, kneed grass.
knoll: A little round hill; a mound; a small elevation of earth; the top or crown of a hill. On knoll or hillock rears his crest, Lonely and huge, the giant oak. Sir W. Scott. | To ring, as a bell; to strike a knell upon; to toll; to proclaim, or summon, by ringing. "Knolled to church." Shak. Heavy clocks knolling the drowsy hours. Tennyson.
knead: 1. To work and press into a mass, usually with the hands; esp., to work, as by repeated pressure with the knuckles, into a well mixed mass, as the materials of bread, cake, etc.; as, to knead dough. The kneading, the making of the cake, the heating of the oven, and the baking. Shak. 2. Fig.: To treat or form as by kneading; to beat. I will knead him : I'll make him supple.
knighthood: 1. The character, dignity, or condition of a knight, or of knights as a class; hence, chivalry. "O shame to knighthood." Shak. If you needs must write, write Cæsar's praise; You 'll gain at least a knighthood, or the bays. Pope. 2. The whole body of knights. The knighthood nowadays are nothing like the knighthood of old time. Chapman.
knubs: Waste silk formed in winding off the threads from a cocoon.
knowall: One who knows everything; hence, one who makes pretension to great knowledge; a wiseacre; -- usually ironical. [Colloq. or R.]
kneck: The twisting of a rope or cable, as it is running out. [Eng.]
knickerbockers: The name for a style of short breeches; smallclothes.
knuff: A lout; a clown. (old) The country knuffs, Hob, Dick, and Hick, With clubs and clouted shoon. Hayward.
knout: A kind of whip for flogging criminals, formerly much used in Russia. The last is a tapering bundle of leather thongs twisted with wire and hardened, so that it mangles the flesh. | To punish with the knout Brougham.
knotwort: A small, herbaceous, trailing plant, of the genus Illecebrum (I. verticillatum.)
knockkneed: Having the legs bent inward so that the knees touch in walking. [Written also knack-kneed.]
knot: 1. (a) A fastening together of the pars or ends of one or more threads, cords, ropes, etc., by any one of various ways of tying or entangling. (b) A lump or loop formed in a thread, cord, rope. | 1. To tie in or with, or form into, a knot or knots; to form a knot on, as a rope; to entangle. "Knotted curls." Drayton. As tight as I could knot the noose. Tennyson. 2. To unite closely;
knighttemplar: See Commandery, n., 3, and also Templar, n., 1 and 3.
knack: 1. To crack; to make a sharp, abrupt noise to chink. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Bp. Hall. 2. To speak affectedly. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell. | 1. A petty contrivance; a toy; a plaything; a knickknack. A knack, a toy, a trick, a baby's cap. Shak. 2. A readiness in performance; aptness at doing something; skill; facility; dexterity.
kneadingly: In the manner of one kneading.
knocking: A beating; a rap; a series of raps. The . . . repeated knockings of the head upon the ground by the Chinese worshiper. H. Spencer.
knife: 1. An instrument consisting of a thin blade, usually of steel and having a sharp edge for cutting, fastened to a handle, but of many different forms and names for different uses; | 1. (Hort.) To prune with the knife. 2. To cut or stab with a knife. [Low]
knapsack: A case of canvas or leather, for carrying on the back a soldier's necessaries, or the clothing, etc., of a traveler. And each one fills his knapsack or his scrip With some rare thing that on the field is found. Drayton.
knarl: A knot in wood. See Gnarl.
knitchet: A number of things tied or knit together; a bundle; a fagot. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Halliwell. When they [stems of asphodel] be dried, they ought to be made up into knitchets, or handfuls. Holland.
knotty: 1. Full of knots; knotted; having many knots; as, knotty timber; a knotty rope. 2. Hard; rugged; as, a knotty head. Rewe. 3. Difficult; intricate; perplexed. A knotty point to which we now proceed Pope.
knighterrantry: The character or actions of wandering knights; the practice of wandering in quest of adventures; chivalry; a quixotic or romantic adventure or scheme. The rigid guardian [i. e., conscience] of a blameless heart Is weak with rank knight-erratries o'errun. Young.
knotberry: The cloudberry (Rudus Chamæmorus); -- so called from its knotted stems.
knockout: Act of knocking out, or state of being knocked out. | That knocks out; characterized by knocking out; as, a knock-out blow; a knock-out key for knocking out a drill from a collet.
knowable: That may be known; capable of being discovered, understood, or ascertained. Thus mind and matter, as known or knowable, are only two different series of phenomena or qualities. Sir W. Hamilton.
knitback: The plant comfrey; -- so called from its use as a restorative. Dr. Prier.
knawel: A low, spreading weed (Scleranthus annuus), common in sandy soil.
knop: 1. A knob; a bud; a bunch; a button. Four bowls made like unto almonds, with their knops and their flowers. Ex. xxv. 21. 2. (Arch.) Any boldly projecting sculptured ornament; esp., the ornamental termination of a pinnacle, and then synonymous with finial; -- called also knob, and knosp. Knop sedge (Bot.), the bur reed (Sparganium);
kneecap: 1. (Anat.) The kneepan. 2. A cap or protection for the knee.
knickerbocker: A linsey-woolsey fabric having a rough knotted surface on the right side; used for women's dresses.
knittle: 1. A string that draws together a purse or bag. [Prov. Eng.] Wright. 2. pl. (Naut.) See Nettles.
knighterrant: A wandering knight; a knight who traveled in search of adventures, for the purpose of exhibiting military skill, prowess, and generosity.
kneel: To bend the knee; to fall or rest on the knees; -- sometimes with down. And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. Acts vii. 60. As soon as you are dressed, kneel and say the Lord's Prayer. Jer. Taylor.
knightmarshal: An officer in the household of the British sovereign, who has cognizance of transgressions within the royal household and verge, and of contracts made there, a member of the household being one of the parties. Wharton.
knottiness: 1. The quality or state of being knotty or full of knots. 2. Difficulty of solution; intricacy; complication. " Knottiness of his style." Hare.
knurled: 1. Full of knots; gnarled. 2. Milled, as the head of a screw, or the edge of a coin.
knavishness: The quality or state of being knavish; knavery; dishonesty.
knotgrass: (a) a common weed with jointed stems (Polygonum aviculare); knotweed. (b) The dog grass. See under Dog. Note: An infusion of Polygonum aviculare was once supposed to have the effect of stopping the growth of an animal, and hence it was called, as by Shakespeare, "hindering knotgrass." We want a boy extremely for this function, Kept under for a year with milk and knotgrass.
knownothingism: The doctrines, principles, or practices, of the Know-nothings.
knitster: A woman who knits. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
knobbing: Rough dressing by knocking off knobs or projections.
kneejoint: 1. The joint of the knee. 2. (Mach.) A toggle joint; -- so called because consisting of two pieces jointed to each other end to end, making an angle like the knee when bent.
knightliness: The character or bearing suitable for a knight; chivalry. Spenser.
knurl: A contorted knot in wood; a crossgrained protuberance; a nodule; a boss or projection. 2. One who, or that which, is crossgrained. | To provide with ridges, to assist the grasp, as in the edge of a flat knob, or coin; to mill.
knighterratic: Pertaining to a knight-errant or to knight-errantry. Quart. Rev.
knopped: Having knops or knobs; fastened as with buttons. (old) Rom. of R.
knownothing: A member of a secret political organization in the United States, the chief objects of which were the proscription of foreigners by the repeal of the naturalization laws, and the exclusive choice of native Americans for office. Note: The party originated in 1853, and existed for about three years.
knightly: Of or pertaining to a knight; becoming a knight; chivalrous; as, a knightly combat; a knightly spirit. For knightly jousts and fierce encounters fit. Spenser. [Excuses] full knightly without scorn. | In a manner becoming a knight. And why thou comest thus knightly clad in arms. Shak.
kneebrush: 1. (Zoöl.) A tuft or brush of hair on the knees of some species of antelopes and other animals; -- chiefly used in the plural. 2. (Zoöl.) A thick mass or collection of hairs on the legs of bees, by aid of which they carry the collected pollen to the hive or nest; -- usually in the plural.
knockdown: A felling by a knock, as of a combatant, or of an animal. | Of force sufficient to fell or completely overthrow; as, a knockdown blow; a knockdown argument. [Colloq.]
kneedeep: 1. Rising to the knees; knee-high; as, water or snow knee-deep. Grass knee-deep within a month. Milton. 2. Sunk to the knees; as, men knee-deep in water. Where knee-deep the trees were standing. Longfellow.
knowledge: 1. The act or state of knowing; clear perception of fact, truth, or duty; certain apprehension; familiar cognizance; cognition. Knowledge, which is the highest degree of the speculative faculties,… | To acknowledge. (old) "Sinners which knowledge their sins." Tyndale.
knightbachelor: A knight of the most ancient, but lowest, order of English knights, and not a member of any order of chivalry. See Bachelor, 4.
knag: 1. A knot in wood; a protuberance. Wright. 2. A wooden peg for hanging things on. Wright. 3. The prong of an antler Holland. 4. The rugged top of a hill. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
knabble: To bite or nibble. (old) Horses will knabble at walls, and rats gnaw iron. Sir T. Browne.
knocker: One who, or that which, knocks; specifically, an instrument, or kind of hammer, fastened to a door, to be used in seeking for admittance. Shut, shut the door, good John ! fatigued, knocker; say I'm sick, I'm dead. Pope.
knightage: To body of knights, taken collectively.
knee: 1. In man, the joint in the middle part of the leg. 2. (Anat.) (a) The joint, or region of the joint, between the thigh and leg. (b) In the horse and allied animals, the carpal joint, corresponding… | To supplicate by kneeling. (old) Fall down, and knee The way into his mercy. Shak
knobkerrie: A short club with a knobbed end used as a missile weapon by Kafir and other native tribes of South Africa.
knappy: Having knaps; full of protuberances or humps; knobby. (old) Huloet.
knarred: Knotty; gnarled. The knarred and crooked cedar knees. Longfellow.
knaggy: Knotty; rough; figuratively, rough in temper. Fuller. -- Knag"gi*ness, n.
knave: 1. A boy; especially, a boy servant. (old) Wyclif. Chaucer. O murderous slumber, Lay'st thou thy leaden mace upon my boy That plays thee music Gentle knave, good night. Shak. 2. Any male servant; a menial. (old) Chaucer. He's but Fortune's knave, A minister of her will. Shak. 3. A tricky, deceitful fellow; a dishonest person; a rogue; a villain.
knob: 1. A hard protuberance; a hard swelling or rising; a bunch; a lump; as, a knob in the flesh, or on a bone. 2. A knoblike ornament or handle; as, the knob of a lock, door, or drawer. Chaucer. 3. | To grow into knobs or bunches; to become knobbed. (old) Drant.
knobstick: One who refuses to join, or withdraws from, a trades union. [Cant, Eng.]
knuckle: 1. The joint of a finger, particularly when made prominent by the closing of the fingers. Davenant. 2. The kneejoint, or middle joint, of either leg of a quadruped, especially of a calf; | To yield; to submit; -- used with down, to, or under. To knuckle to. (a) To submit to in a contest; to yield to. [Colloq.] See To knock under, under Knock, v. i. (b) To apply one's self vigorously or…
knickknack: A trifle or toy; a bawble; a gewgaw.
knapple: To break off with an abrupt, sharp noise; to bite; to nibble. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]
knockabout: 1. Marked by knocking about or roughness. 2. Of noisy and violent character. [Theat. Slang] 3. Characterized by, or suitable for, knocking about, or traveling or wandering hither and thither. 4. | 1. (Naut.) A small yacht, generally from fifteen to twenty-five feet in length, having a mainsail and a jib. All knockabouts have ballast and either a keel or centerboard.
kneepiece: A piece shaped like a knee; as, the kneepieces or ears of a boat. KNEIPPISM; KNEIPP'S CURE; KNEIPP CURE Kneipp"ism, n. Also Kneipp's, or Kneipp, cure. Treatment of disease by forms of hydrotherapy, as walking barefoot in the morning dew, baths, wet compresses, cold affusions, etc.; -- so called from its originator, Sebastian Kneipp (1821-97), a German priest.
knapweed: The black centaury (Centaurea nigra); -- so called from the knoblike heads of flowers. Called also bullweed.
knightbanneret: A knight who carried a banner, who possessed fiefs to a greater amount than the knight bachelor, and who was obliged to serve in war with a greater number of attendants. The dignity was sometimes conferred by the sovereign in person on the field of battle.
knight: 1. A young servant or follower; a military attendant. (old) 2. (a) In feudal times, a man-at-arms serving on horseback and admitted to a certain military rank with special ceremonies, including an… | To dub or create (one) a knight; -- done in England by the sovereign only, who taps the kneeling candidate with a sword, saying: Rise, Sir ---. A soldier, by the honor-giving hand Of Cknighted in the…
kneeler: 1. One who kneels or who worships by or while kneeling. Tennyson. 2. A cushion or stool to kneel on. 3. (Eccl. Hist.) A name given to certain catechumens and penitents who were permitted to join only in parts of church worship.
knock: 1. To drive or be driven against something; to strike against something; to clash; as, one heavy body knocks against another. Bacon. 2. To strike or beat with something hard or heavy; to rap; | 1. To strike with something hard or heavy; to move by striking; to drive (a thing) against something; as, to knock a ball with a bat; to knock the head against a post; to knock a lamp off the table.
knebelite: A mineral of a gray, red, brown, or green color, and glistening luster. It is a silicate of iron and manganese.
knowableness: The state or quality of being knowable. Locke.
kneejerk: A jerk or kick produced by a blow or sudden strain upon the patellar tendon of the knee, which causes a sudden contraction of the quadriceps muscle.
knotless: Free from knots; without knots. "Silver firs with knotless trunks." Congreve.
knowingness: The state or quality of being knowing or intelligent; shrewdness; skillfulness.
